2 Corinthians 1.summary: Paul and Timothy greet the believers in Corinth and throughout Achaia (2 Corinthians 1:1–2). Paul praises God as the source of mercy and comfort: the consolation he receives in affliction enables him to help others (2 Corinthians 1:3–7). He describes a severe ordeal in Asia that made him despair of life and taught him to rely on God who raises the dead; he requests their prayers (2 Corinthians 1:8–11). Defending his sincerity, Paul explains his changed travel itinerary and insists that his message about Christ is not unreliable, because God’s promises find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:12–22). He says he delayed returning to Corinth to spare them a painful encounter, not to dominate their faith (2 Corinthians 1:23–24). The chapter introduces the letter’s intertwined concerns: suffering, trust, strained relationships, and the integrity of apostolic ministry.
2 Corinthians 1.whereWeAre: The opening references a difficult but unspecified crisis in Asia (1:8) and a change of plans involving Macedonia and Corinth (1:15–16). The precise incident cannot be identified from surviving evidence. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 1 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 2.summary: Paul explains that he chose not to make another sorrowful visit and had written with tears so that the Corinthians would recognize his love (2 Corinthians 2:1–4). He urges the congregation to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love for someone who has caused grief and received punishment from the majority (2 Corinthians 2:5–11). The person is unnamed here, and identifying the incident with 1 Corinthians 5 remains uncertain. Paul recounts finding an opening for gospel work in Troas but leaving for Macedonia because he could not find (Titus 2) Corinthians 2:12–13. He then celebrates God’s leading in Christ, describing the gospel ministry through the image of a fragrance perceived differently by those who respond and those who do not (2 Corinthians 2:14–17). The chapter presents restoration after discipline alongside Paul’s vulnerability and responsibility to proclaim sincerely.
2 Corinthians 2.whereWeAre: The chapter presupposes an earlier painful encounter and letter, but their full details are not extant. Troas and Macedonia were important sites on Paul’s Aegean travel network. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 2 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

keyFigures.name: Paul

2 Corinthians 3.summary: Paul rejects the suggestion that he needs letters of recommendation: the Corinthian community itself is a letter from Christ, written not with ink but by the Spirit on human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:1–3). He attributes his ministry’s adequacy to God and contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit who gives life (2 Corinthians 3:4–6). Using the giving of the Law and Moses’ radiant face as images, he compares a glorious but passing ministry associated with condemnation to the surpassing and lasting glory of the Spirit’s ministry (2 Corinthians 3:7–11). He discusses the veil in Moses’ story and speaks of its removal in turning to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:12–16). The chapter closes with freedom and transformation as believers behold the Lord’s glory (2 Corinthians 3:17–18). Interpretations of the covenant contrast differ; it should not be turned into a sweeping claim that Jewish people are uniformly spiritually blind.
2 Corinthians 3.whereWeAre: Paul draws directly on Exodus 34:29–35 and prophetic language of an inwardly written covenant (compare Jeremiah 31:31–34), while addressing the status of his ministry in a mixed first-century Christian congregation. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 3 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 4.summary: Paul says that because ministry comes through God’s mercy, he refuses deceitful methods or manipulation of the message (2 Corinthians 4:1–2). Although some do not recognize the gospel, Paul proclaims Jesus Christ as Lord and describes the God who commanded light at creation as shining in hearts through knowledge of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:3–6). This treasure is held in fragile clay jars so that the extraordinary power is understood to come from God rather than from human strength (2 Corinthians 4:7). He lists pressures, persecution, and hardships that do not finally destroy him and relates his suffering to making Jesus’ life visible (2 Corinthians 4:8–12). Paul trusts the God who raised Jesus and anticipates thanksgiving spreading through the community (2 Corinthians 4:13–15). He concludes that present suffering, real though it is, does not exhaust the story: inward renewal and hope orient attention toward what is unseen and lasting (2 Corinthians 4:16–18).
2 Corinthians 4.whereWeAre: The letter reflects the vulnerability of itinerant teachers in Roman provincial society, where travel, poverty, public criticism, and imprisonment were real possibilities; the exact troubles listed are not individually dated. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 4 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 5.summary: Continuing his reflection on mortality, Paul compares the present body to an earthly tent and longs for a lasting dwelling from God (2 Corinthians 5:1–5). He expresses confidence while living by faith rather than sight, acknowledging a longing to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6–8). Because all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat, he seeks to please Christ and persuade others sincerely (2 Corinthians 5:9–13). Christ’s love constrains him: one died for all, and those who live are called not to live merely for themselves (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). Paul declares that in Christ there is new creation and that God has entrusted the message of reconciliation to his ambassadors (2 Corinthians 5:16–20). The final verse connects Christ’s sinlessness, his bearing of sin, and believers’ becoming God’s righteousness in him (2 Corinthians 5:21). Christians differ about some details of Paul’s imagery of embodiment and the exact theological account of atonement.
2 Corinthians 5.whereWeAre: Paul’s statements address mortality, apostolic credibility, and communal alienation in the first-century churches rather than offering a full chronological account of the afterlife. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 5 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 6.summary: Paul appeals to his hearers not to receive God’s grace in vain, citing the time of divine favor and salvation (2 Corinthians 6:1–2). He describes the effort to give no needless offense while enduring afflictions, beatings, imprisonments, sleeplessness, and hunger; he also names patience, sincere love, truthful speech, and God’s power (2 Corinthians 6:3–10). The string of contrasts—sorrowful yet rejoicing, poor yet enriching many—underscores how paradoxical his ministry looks (2 Corinthians 6:8–10). Addressing the Corinthians openly, he asks them to widen their hearts toward him (2 Corinthians 6:11–13). He then warns against unequal partnership with unbelief, contrasting righteousness with lawlessness and God’s temple with idols (2 Corinthians 6:14–18). The passage’s precise application to marriage, civic relationships, and other associations is debated; its explicit imagery centers on holiness and worship.
2 Corinthians 6.whereWeAre: Paul is defending an embattled mission in Greek-speaking Roman cities. Scholars debate whether 6:14–7:1 originated as part of the surrounding appeal, although it stands in the canonical letter. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 6 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 7.summary: Paul begins by urging purification in light of God’s promises (2 Corinthians 7:1), then resumes his appeal for the Corinthians to receive him with open hearts (2 Corinthians 7:2–4). He describes fears and troubles upon arriving in Macedonia but says God comforted him through Titus’s arrival and the news Titus brought of the Corinthians’ concern (2 Corinthians 7:5–7). Although his earlier letter caused sorrow, Paul rejoices that their grief led to repentance rather than lasting harm (2 Corinthians 7:8–10). He distinguishes godly grief, which results in earnest action, from sorrow that does not lead to life; he lists the Corinthians’ renewed concern as evidence of a serious response (2 Corinthians 7:11–12). The meeting with Titus reinforces mutual encouragement and confidence (2 Corinthians 7:13–16). The chapter presents painful correction, when handled rightly, as a possible path to repaired relationships, not an excuse for coercive humiliation.
2 Corinthians 7.whereWeAre: The letter refers to a difficult prior communication, travel through Macedonia, and Titus’s mission, but does not fully reconstruct the sequence of all visits and letters. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 7 addresses reconciliation, suffering, and the credibility of Paul’s ministry.

2 Corinthians 8.summary: Paul turns to the collection for believers in need, holding up the Macedonian churches as examples: despite severe testing and poverty, they gave generously and voluntarily (2 Corinthians 8:1–5). He urges Titus to help the Corinthians complete the contribution they had already begun (2 Corinthians 8:6–7). Rather than issuing a bare command, he appeals to the sincerity of love and to Christ, who became poor so that others might become rich through his grace (2 Corinthians 8:8–9). He asks the Corinthians to finish according to their means, emphasizing willingness and a fair sharing of resources, not an impossible burden (2 Corinthians 8:10–15). Paul thanks God for Titus’s concern and explains that trusted representatives will oversee the gift so that the collection is administered honorably before God and people (2 Corinthians 8:16–24). The chapter connects generosity with integrity, equal concern, and practical financial accountability.
2 Corinthians 8.whereWeAre: Paul’s collection was intended for believers in Jerusalem (see 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Romans 15:25–27). The exact participants and the status of every local contribution cannot be established independently. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 8 addresses the Jerusalem collection and trusted delegates.

2 Corinthians 9.summary: Paul continues discussing the gift for believers in need. He says that the Corinthians’ earlier readiness has encouraged others, but he sends representatives ahead so that the promised contribution will be prepared and freely given rather than hurriedly extracted (2 Corinthians 9:1–5). Using agricultural imagery, he teaches that sowing sparingly and generously leads to corresponding harvests, while emphasizing that each giver should decide in the heart, without reluctance or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). He says God can provide sufficiency for good works and connects generosity to righteousness, thanksgiving, and the needs of recipients (2 Corinthians 9:8–12). The gift will also demonstrate the Corinthians’ profession of the gospel and deepen bonds of prayer and gratitude (2 Corinthians 9:13–15). The passage encourages generosity, not a guaranteed formula for personal wealth.
2 Corinthians 9.whereWeAre: The collection linking Achaia, Macedonia, and Jerusalem required coordination and advance notice. Paul’s language about Achaia’s readiness shows the mutual expectations among participating churches. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 9 addresses the Jerusalem collection and trusted delegates.

2 Corinthians 10.summary: Paul begins a sharper defense of his ministry, appealing through Christ’s gentleness while acknowledging accusations that he is timid in person but bold from afar (2 Corinthians 10:1–2). He says that although he lives as a human being, his struggle is not conducted with worldly weapons; he speaks metaphorically of overthrowing arguments that resist the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:3–6). He asks the Corinthians to look beyond outward impressions and reminds them that his authority is for building up, not tearing down (2 Corinthians 10:7–11). Paul rejects self-congratulatory comparison with others and refuses to claim work outside the sphere assigned to him (2 Corinthians 10:12–16). He concludes that boasting should be in the Lord and that true approval comes from God rather than self-praise (2 Corinthians 10:17–18). The chapter challenges rhetorical status competition and attempts to discredit Paul through appearance or speaking style.
2 Corinthians 10.whereWeAre: In the Greco-Roman world, public speakers were evaluated for presence, rhetorical polish, and recognized status. Paul’s critics exploit these expectations, though their identities remain unknown. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 10 addresses competing claims to authority, hardship, and plans for accountability.

2 Corinthians 11.summary: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with his seemingly foolish speech as he expresses protective concern that they remain devoted to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:1–4). He questions the claims of those he sarcastically calls superior apostles and says that although he is not a polished speaker, he is not lacking in knowledge (2 Corinthians 11:5–6). He explains his decision not to require payment from Corinth for his preaching, noting support from other churches and contrasting his conduct with rivals (2 Corinthians 11:7–15). Continuing an intentionally ironic “boast,” he compares credentials and then lists imprisonment, beatings, shipwrecks, journeys, danger, deprivation, and ongoing concern for churches (2 Corinthians 11:16–29). Rather than treating suffering as a badge of social rank, he concludes by boasting in weakness and recounts his escape from Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). The chapter reveals the costly and contested character of Paul’s ministry.
2 Corinthians 11.whereWeAre: Paul’s rival teachers are not named and their exact origin is debated. The reference to Aretas IV and an ethnarch at Damascus (11:32) has prompted historical discussion, but the local administrative arrangement is uncertain. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 11 addresses competing claims to authority, hardship, and plans for accountability.

2 Corinthians 12.summary: Paul continues his reluctant boasting by speaking in the third person about a man in Christ who was caught up to the third heaven and paradise fourteen years earlier; he does not claim to know whether the experience was bodily (2 Corinthians 12:1–6). He then describes a “thorn in the flesh,” without identifying it, and reports that his request for its removal was answered with the assurance that divine grace is sufficient and power is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Paul insists that he seeks the Corinthians themselves, not their possessions, and compares his affection to a parent’s responsibility toward children (2 Corinthians 12:11–15). He denies exploiting them through Titus or other representatives (2 Corinthians 12:16–18). He says his defense is aimed at building them up and fears arriving to find quarrels, jealousy, disorder, and unresolved sexual wrongdoing (2 Corinthians 12:19–21). The passage warns against confident guesses about the thorn’s nature.
2 Corinthians 12.whereWeAre: Ancient Jewish and early Christian writings sometimes used layered-heaven imagery. Paul refers to a revelation fourteen years earlier, but neither its calendar date nor the nature of his “thorn” is established. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 12 addresses competing claims to authority, hardship, and plans for accountability.

2 Corinthians 13.summary: Paul announces that a forthcoming journey would be his third visit to Corinth and refers to the requirement that charges be established by two or three witnesses (2 Corinthians 13:1–2). He warns that he will not overlook persistent wrongdoing, explaining that Christ was crucified in weakness yet lives by God’s power; Paul’s own ministry participates in this pattern (2 Corinthians 13:3–4). Rather than continuing to demand proof from Paul alone, he urges the Corinthians to examine themselves regarding their faith (2 Corinthians 13:5–6). He prays that they will do what is right even if he appears unimpressive and stresses that his authority is to build up, not destroy (2 Corinthians 13:7–10). The letter ends with calls for joy, restoration, encouragement, agreement, and peace, followed by greetings and a blessing naming the grace of Jesus Christ, God’s love, and fellowship of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:11–14). The ending seeks repair rather than a permanent rupture.
2 Corinthians 13.whereWeAre: The letter anticipates another visit but does not document the outcome in this chapter. The previous visit sequence is partly reconstructable from Paul’s letters, yet not every detail is agreed. These circumstances illuminate why 2 Corinthians 13 addresses competing claims to authority, hardship, and plans for accountability.
